entries.modern_form: PIE *h₂ep- 'water, body of water' (Pokorny 2. ap-/āp- 'Wasser, Fluß', IEW 51-52; the collateral form ab- 'Wasser, Fluß' at IEW 1)
entries.note: The root is real and the gloss 'water' is right; 'Indo-European' is the correct language label. Nourai's double headword 'Ab 1, Ap 1' reproduces Pokorny's own two-entry treatment: IEW p.1 has 'ab- "Wasser, Fluß"' (Lat. amnis < *abnis, OIr. ab/abann, W. afon), IEW pp.51-52 has '2. āp- "Wasser, Fluß"' (Skt. āpaḥ, Av. āfš/āpəm, OPers. āpi-, NPers. āb, Lith. upė, OPruss. ape), and Pokorny explicitly links them (p.52: 'Daneben kelt.-lat. ab-, s. u. ab-'). Modern reconstruction is a single *h₂ep-; Latin amnis and OIr. ab are now normally taken from an -n- stem *h₂ep-h₃on-/*h₂ep-n- of that same root rather than from an independent *ab-, so 'Ab' as a separate root is no longer maintained, but it is not a wrong word — only a superseded analysis. Nourai's own page reference POK:1 lands on the Celtic/Italic half; his whole Iranian chain sits on IEW 51-52, which he does not cite here. NOTE ON THE CHART AS A WHOLE: the Persian branch on this page is Paul Horn's 1893 analysis (āb 'Glanz' as the first element of āftāb, ābrū), and the Arabic branch is Addi Shir's 1908 claim that Arabic أبهة is Persian آب بها. Both were already doubted in the 19th c. (Hübschmann) and are rejected by current Iranian and Arabic lexicography (Cheung 2007; Asbaghi 1988).

ref_check.note: POK_01.txt form-feed leaf 8 = printed p.1 (offset leaf = p+8): 'ab- "Wasser, Fluß". Lat. amnis f., später m. (*abnis); air. ab (*abā) Gen. abae "Fluß", daneben abann, cymr. afon … WP. I 46 f.' — the page confirms an IE root ab- 'water, river', so the root box and its gloss are supported. But this page contains NO Indo-Iranian material: Avestan/Old Persian/New Persian āp/āb are at POK pp.51-52 (leaf 59-60), '2. āp- "Wasser, Fluß": Ai. āp- f. "Wasser" … av. Nom. Sg. āfš, Akk. Sg. āpəm … Daneben kelt.-lat. ab-, s. u. ab-.' Nourai cites only the first page, hence 'partial'.

nodes.derivation: PIE *h₂ep- (Pokorny 2. āp-) → Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hā́ps → Proto-Iranian *Hā́fš, a root noun in -p-. In Avestan the nominative singular shows the regular Iranian devoicing of *-p-s to -fš (YAv. āfš), while the oblique stem keeps the labial: acc. sg. āpəm, gen. pl. apąm; the Waters are personified (Ābān Yašt, Y. 65 Āpąm Nəpāt). Old Persian has the i-extended stem āpi- (Bīsutūn 1.19 apiyā 'into the water', 1.95 āpiš). In Middle Persian the Avestan/OP form is continued as āp/āb, written ʾp̄ in Book Pahlavi (Aramaic ideogram MYA 'water'), ʾb in Manichaean, which is exactly what Nourai's node 'âp' represents; intervocalic and final Iranian -p- lenites to -b/-w in Middle and New Persian, giving NP āb (Pāzand āw). So one label covering Avestan and Pahlavi 'āp' is legitimate: the Pahlavi book-form is still written with the p-grapheme.

nodes.derivation: (a) āb «آب ۲» 'glitter, lustre': the words are real and the sense is real — classical Persian āb means 'sheen, water (of a sword or a pearl), freshness, honour' beside 'water', and Wiktionary lists 'honour, reputation, standing' as sense 5 of āb itself, i.e. as a metaphorical extension of āb 'water' (the glint of a water surface, the 'water' of a blade), not as a separate lexeme. Horn set it up as a separate lemma no. 3 āb 'Glanz' compared with Skt. ābhā- 'Glanz', but in his own footnote conceded 'Die Zusammenstellung von np. āb und skr. ābhā- ist keineswegs sicher; von der Bedeutung "(glitzernder) Wasserspiegel" könnte man sehr leicht zu "Glanz" kommen' — which is Nourai's derivation. Hübschmann §75a repeats that the equation with ābhā- is 'unsicher'. So treating «آب ۲» as the water word used metaphorically is the better-supported view and Nourai's edge #1→#2 stands. (b) ābrū «آبرو» 'good repute': a transparent Persian compound āb + rū(y) 'face' (shortened from āb-i rūy), literally 'water of the face', paralleled by Kurdish avrû/awrrû. But the received Persian reading of the literal sense is 'the water/sweat of the face' — Mo'in glosses آب‌رخ and آب‌رو first as 'عرق، خوی' (sweat) and only then as 'اعتبار، قدر، جاه، شرف، عرض، ناموس' — not Nourai's 'facial shine'. Route: no Middle Persian *āb-rōy is attested; the compound is a New Persian formation, current from the earliest classical poetry. (c) āftāb «آفتاب» 'sun': this is where the chart is wrong. āftāb does not contain āb. It continues Middle Persian ʾptʾb /āftāb/ 'sunshine' (Parthian ʾbdʾb /ābdāb/ 'sunshine'), from Proto-Iranian *abi-tāpah = the preverb *abi- 'on, upon' (Av. aiwi-, OP abiy-) + the root *tap- 'to be hot, to shine' (Av. tāpaiieiti, BMP tʾp- 'to heat, burn, shine'). Iranian *-bit- gave MP -ft- regularly (*abi-tāpa- > āftāb, cf. the same preverb in āfrīn < *abi-θrai-, āfarīdan), so the first syllable is a prefix, not the noun āb; the parallel Parthian ābdāb with -d- shows the preverb, not 'water'. Nourai simply inherits Horn's 1893 grouping (Horn lists af-tāb among the compounds of his āb 'Glanz'), and Mo'in's dictionary repeats it ('آفتاب [آب + تاب: جرم روشن گرمابخش]'), but Cheung's Etymological Dictionary of the Iranian Verb (2007) s.v. *tap and the Manichaean dictionary evidence settle it against them.

ref_check.note: Horn, Grundriss p.1 (HRN.txt form-feed leaf 22, offset leaf = printed + 21) is exactly the page Nourai used. It has '2. āb, āw "Wasser" … ap. āp- "Wasser"; aw. āp-; phlv. āp (pāz. āw); ai. āp-, kurd. āw; afγ. ōba (fem.); bel. ap, n. āf' and then '3. āb "Glanz" (Šāhn. I S. 14 Vers 7), vergl. āb|rū, āb|tāb, āb|mend, Rōd|ābe, Suhr|āb, Mihr|āb, Ardā Vīr|āf, af|tāb, phlv. āb; skr. ābhā- "Glanz". afγ. bel. LW. āb, ābrū; kurd. LW. āwrū.' So Horn is the source both for the separate lemma āb 'Glanz' and for filing ābrū and āftāb under it — Nourai's node is a faithful copy. Horn's own footnote 2 on the same page, however, undercuts half of it: 'Die Zusammenstellung von np. āb und skr. ābhā- ist keineswegs sicher; von der Bedeutung "(glitzernder) Wasserspiegel" könnte man sehr leicht zu "Glanz" kommen.'

AEF = Jalāl Khāleqi Motlaq, Asās-e Eštteqāq-e Fārsi vol. I (Bonyād-e Farhang-e Irān 1356/1977), which is the Persian rendering of Horn's Grundriss with Hübschmann's notes. refs_online.json records it as not online (no archive.org / noorlib copy; 2015 Mehrāfrūz reprint print-only) and there is no local text. Since it is Horn in Persian dress, its p.2 will be Horn's nos. 2-3, i.e. the same content already checked under HRN:1.

consulted.note: 'Da āb "Glanz" == skr. ābhā- H. 3 unsicher ist, so ergiebt sich, dass ap. w nur vor r sicher zu np. b wird.' Hübschmann rejects Horn's Sanskrit comparison for āb 'Glanz' — which removes the only reason to keep it apart from āb 'water', and so indirectly supports Nourai's edge while contradicting the separate-lexeme framing.

nodes.derivation: The Arabic word itself is real: أُبَّهَة ubbaha 'pomp, splendour, grandeur, majesty' (Nourai's 'abboha'), a fuʿʿala-pattern noun. What is disputed is where it comes from. Nourai's second form 'âb-bahâ' is not an Arabic word at all but Addi Shir's proposed Persian etymon آب بها, i.e. āb 'lustre' + bahā 'splendour, worth' — so the node's language label 'Arabic' fits only the second word. Addi Shir (1908) claimed Arabic al-ubbaha was 'muʿarrab' (Arabicised) from that Persian phrase, and Nourai builds his chart on him. Modern Arabic lexicography assigns أُبَّهَة to the native triliteral root ء ب ه (ʔ-b-h), the root of the verb أَبِهَ 'to pay heed, take notice (of), be mindful', with the abstract 'self-regard, consequence' > 'grandeur' — no borrowing involved. Decisively, Asya Asbaghi's Persische Lehnwörter im Arabischen (1988), the standard modern inventory of Persian loans in Arabic, does not list it: her ʾab- entries run ābaq, ablaq, āblūǧ, ʾabūz, abū-zarǧmihr, ʾabhar, ʾabharī, ʾabīraǧ, with no ubbaha. Neither al-Jawālīqī's al-Muʿarrab nor al-ʿUnaysī's Tafsīr al-alfāẓ al-dakhīla contains it either. Phonologically the Persian source is also awkward: a two-word phrase āb bahā would not be expected to yield the geminated fuʿʿala shape ubbaha. The edge #2→#3 should be regarded as an Addi Shir folk-etymology.

ref_check.note: Addi Shir does say it, on the second page of the hamza chapter. AFM_pages.txt line 182 (form-feed leaf 8; leaf 7 is the chapter opening باب الهمزة, so leaf 8 ≈ printed p.6-7, matching Nourai's citation): '( الأبهة ) العظمة والبهجة معرب آب بها' — 'al-ubbaha: greatness and splendour, Arabicised from āb bahā'. (The OCR of this line reads '+ لي العظمة والبهجة معرب أب بآ'; the surrounding entries are ابزيم/ابزن, أباش/البوش, ابر 'cloud' < Pers. abr.) The same chapter opens with '( الأباب ) الماء … معرب آب وهو الماء'. So the chart faithfully reports its source; the source is what is unreliable.

nodes.derivation: New Persian ابهت obbahat (more usually transcribed ubbahat/obbahat) 'grandeur, majesty, imposing presence' is a straightforward loan from Arabic أُبَّهَة ubbaha, taken over with the tāʾ marbūṭa realised as a full -t, which is the normal Persian treatment of Arabic feminines in -a when they are borrowed in the construct-like 'pausal-t' shape (cf. NP قدرت qodrat, رحمت raḥmat, نعمت neʿmat). The gemination of the -bb- is kept. So the edge #3→#4, Arabic → Persian, is real and is a genuine re-borrowing of an Arabic word into Persian. What is NOT established is that this is a round trip: it is only a round trip if node #3 is right that the Arabic word was itself Persian آب بها, and modern Arabic and loanword scholarship denies that (see node 3). Two small points on the chart's data: the script «أبهت» is given in Arabic orthography with hamza, whereas Persian normally writes ابهت; and Nourai's gloss 'elegance' is weak — Moʿin has 'بزرگی، بزرگواری، شکوه، عظمت' and Wiktionary 'magnificence, grandeur, imposing presence', i.e. 'grandeur/majesty' rather than 'elegance'.

ref_check.note: Moʿin has the entry and tags it Arabic. MON_part1.txt line 6560 (OCR 'ابسهت' for ابهت): 'ابهت: [ع.] (اِمص.) بزرگی، بزرگواری، شکوه، عظمت، بهجت، شادمانی، نخوت.' — '[Arabic] (abstract noun) greatness, nobility, splendour, magnificence, joy, haughtiness'. The neighbouring headwords are ابهام / ابهام پا (before) and ابهر (after), which is the right alphabetical slot for an early page of vol. I, consistent with p.131. Exact page verification is impossible: the OCR of Moʿin carries no page markers, and refs_online.json records that the online Moʿin text (vajehyab/abadis) cannot be mapped to print pages. Note that Moʿin marks the word simply '[ع.]' = Arabic; he does NOT say the Arabic came from Persian, so he supports the Arabic→Persian edge only, not the round trip.
